A has revenue and total assets of S$450,000 each; B has revenue of S$450,000 and assets of S$520,000. Do they use the same XBRL format, and what PDF attachment does A need?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Evidence verified

**ACRA XBRL financial statement filing requirements and exemptions** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** ACRA says all Singapore-incorporated companies must prepare financial statements, except dormant relevant companies, and must file them unless exempted. A solvent exempt private company may qualify not to file; dormant-relevant-company relief requires all Companies Act section 201A conditions. Newly incorporated or inactive status alone is not listed as an exemption in this guidance. For required filings, ACRA lists simplified XBRL plus an authorised PDF for smaller and non-publicly accountable companies; XBRL FSH (Banks) or XBRL FSH (Insurance) plus an authorised PDF for the regulated bank, finance and insurance group; PDF only for companies limited by guarantee or companies approved to use other standards; and Full XBRL without a separate PDF copy for all other Singapore-incorporated companies required to file financial statements. “Smaller” requires both current-year revenue and assets not exceeding S$500,000. “Non-publicly accountable” also excludes listed and specified regulated entity types. ACRA labels technical resources as applying from 19 October 2026 onwards and identifies ACRA Taxonomy 2026 resources. A company must first determine whether it is required to file financial statements; dormant relevant companies and solvent EPCs may qualify for separate financial-statement exceptions. Small-company revenue and asset thresholds must both be met; group consolidation and currency translation details apply under the ACRA definitions page. The Full/Simplified/FSH/PDF template depends on the company’s exact status and regulatory category. Dormant relevant companies need not prepare/file only if all Companies Act section 201A requirements are met, including the assets, dormancy and listing/subsidiary conditions. A solvent EPC meeting an EPC definition may elect not to file financial statements but may file voluntarily; its annual-return solvency declaration still applies. Foreign companies with Singapore branches and some individually approved cases are addressed elsewhere on the ACRA filing guidance and are not classified by this local-company rule summary. A case-specific conclusion requires: Local/foreign incorporation, company form and whether it is a company limited by guarantee. Required-to-file/exempt status, dormancy history, listed/subsidiary status and group assets. Current-year revenue and assets, consolidation and currency facts. Public-accountability or MAS regulatory status. EPC status and solvency, where relevant. Does not determine an individual company’s template without classification facts. The complete definitions and section 201A eligibility must be checked against ACRA’s linked guidance and law. Do not apply the current page or 19 October 2026 XBRL boundary to a historical filing unless the relevant year-specific official source supports it. Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?

Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.

Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)

Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.

Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.

Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

**Public holiday entitlement and pay** (party in scope: Employee)
- **MOM rule explanation:** An Employment Act-covered employee has 11 paid public holidays each year. If a holiday falls on the rest day, the following working day will be a paid public holiday; if it falls on a non-working day, another day off or an extra day at the gross rate is due. Working on a public holiday ordinarily earns holiday gross pay plus an additional day at the basic rate; overtime applies beyond normal hours. By mutual agreement, the day may be substituted. Part IV coverage limits which employees may use time off in lieu. Distinguish a holiday on a working day, non-working day, or rest day. For holiday gross pay, the employee must not be absent without consent or reasonable excuse on the working day immediately before or after the holiday; authorised leave on either day is permitted. No holiday pay is due when the holiday itself falls during approved unpaid leave. Additional basic-rate pay is the default for working on the holiday; substitute-holiday arrangements require mutual agreement. An employee outside Employment Act coverage is governed by the contract. Time off in lieu of hours worked is available only to employees not covered by Part IV under the stated arrangement. Rest-day pay and any excess-hours overtime are separate entitlements. A case-specific conclusion requires: Employment Act and Part IV coverage. Work schedule and whether the date is a working, non-working or rest day. Whether the employee worked, hours worked, agreed substitution/time-off arrangements, and relevant absence or unpaid-leave facts. Does not decide a specific date’s gazetted holiday status or compute holiday pay without schedule and wage facts. Does not replace separate rest-day, overtime or part-time rules.
